rows.question: My returns are almost zero. Is compounding even happening?
rows.answer: After 12 instalments your SIP is worth ₹12,468 on ₹12,000 put in. Compounding means gains start earning gains, and that needs time to show. Small returns in the early months are common and say little about the long run.

rows.question: My XIRR was very high at first and now it's much lower. Why?
rows.answer: XIRR is a yearly return rate that counts when each instalment went in. In the first year or two it swings a lot, because most of your money has been invested only briefly. A high or low XIRR early on says little about the long run.

rows.question: I've seen almost no returns for months. Is my SIP working?

rows.question: How do I skip one SIP instalment?
rows.answer: On Groww you can change your SIP amount or date anytime, about 2 working days before the debit date, or skip one instalment at a time. Three missed or skipped instalments in a row cancel the SIP.

rows.question: Do I really buy more units when the price is low?
rows.answer: Each month your ₹1,000 buys units at that day's price. When prices were low it bought up to 5.752 units; when high, as few as 5.467. Buying more units when prices are low is how a SIP averages your cost.

rows.question: The app showed 549 but I got only 525 when I redeemed. What happened?
rows.answer: The app shows your value at the latest price (NAV). When you redeem, you get the NAV of the day the request is processed, and prices move every day. So the amount can be a little different from what you saw.

rows.question: Is a SIP different from investing by hand every month?
rows.answer: A SIP invests the same amount automatically every month. Investing by hand works the same way if you do it every month; the SIP just makes it automatic so you don't have to remember or time it.
